title: Three perfect days in Paris, for Paris Photo and the first Christmas lights
dek: Photographs under the glass roof of the Grand Palais, a Latin Quarter Saturday in cold sunshine, and a slow Sunday in the 12th, from the Aligre market to Belmondo at the Cinémathèque.

hero.caption: The Grand Palais, where Paris Photo fills the nave from Thursday to Sunday.

intro:
Paris Photo, the city's big photography fair, opens under the glass roof of the Grand Palais on Thursday, November 12, and runs until Sunday afternoon, so this is the weekend the photography bicentenary reaches its peak. It opens at 13:00 each day, which leaves the mornings for quieter rooms: Tintoretto at the Musée Jacquemart-André on Friday, a 400th-birthday year at the Jardin des Plantes on Saturday, and Belmondo at the Cinémathèque on Sunday.

The season is turning too. The Christmas market in the Tuileries opens on Saturday with its big wheel, the windows at Galeries Lafayette Haussmann are unveiled from Thursday, and the lights go on along the Faubourg Saint-Honoré on Sunday. On Friday night France play South Africa at the Stade de France, so expect rugby shirts on the metro and full bars.

Friday, November 13, is also the eleventh anniversary of the 2015 attacks. Paris marks it quietly, with flowers at the memorial garden on Place Saint-Gervais, which opened last year, and at the plaques outside the Bataclan and the cafés of the 10th and 11th. If you pass one, a moment's pause is the right response.

The plan keeps each day compact: the 8th on Friday, the Latin Quarter on Saturday, the 12th on Sunday. The forecast is cold, dry and sunny for Friday and Saturday, between about 2°C and 9°C, and milder but cloudier on Sunday, which is the day with the most time indoors. It is dark soon after 17:00, so the walks come early.

days.title: Friday: the 8th arrondissement and Paris Photo
days.intro: Two great houses of the Belle Époque, a fair under glass and dinner at an old Aveyron bistro, all within a short walk of the Champs-Élysées.

stops.name: Musée Jacquemart-André: Éternel Tintoret
stops.text: Start in the mansion that Édouard André and Nélie Jacquemart filled with Italian paintings. Until January 24 it holds *Éternel Tintoret*, about thirty paintings and drawings by the Venetian, including *Susanna and the Elders* and *Leda and the Swan*, shown alongside French painters who learned from him, from Delacroix to Ingres. The pairing to look for is Tintoretto's self-portrait hung next to the copy a young Édouard Manet made of it, together for the first time. Tickets are €19; it opens at 10:00, and on Fridays stays open until 21:00.

stops.name: Le Grand Café
stops.text: Lunch in the Grand Palais itself, so you can walk straight into the fair afterwards. The restaurant enters through the Rotonde Clemenceau and runs along the building's flank, which Bonjour Paris's Joy Anderson called "an idyllic urban garden, très Belle Epoque." Order from the seafood bar, or the turbot quenelles or a pepper steak if you want something hot on a cold day. Colin Field, for decades the face of the Hemingway Bar at the Ritz, oversees the drinks. It serves noon to 2:00 a.m. every day, with one menu all day; book for Friday lunch.

stops.name: Paris Photo at the Grand Palais
stops.text: The fair spreads from the nave up to the balconies and into the Salon d'Honneur, with galleries and photobook publishers from around the world selling everything from vintage prints to work made this year. Go in with a plan: walk the nave once without stopping, then return to the stands that caught you. The balconies are calmer and give the best view down over the floor. Paris Photo opens at 13:00 and closes at 20:00 on Friday; tickets are sold online until the fair opens, while they last, so buy before you arrive.

stops.name: Pont Alexandre III at dusk
stops.text: Step out as the light goes. From the Grand Palais it is a few minutes to the Pont Alexandre III, the gilded bridge built for the same 1900 exhibition, and it is at its best just after sunset, when the lamps come on and the dome of the Invalides glows at the far end. Walk to the middle, look back at the glass roof you have just left, then follow the river path west along the Cours la Reine. Wrap up: Friday is forecast dry but cold, with temperatures falling back towards freezing overnight.

stops.name: Chez Savy
stops.text: A short walk from the fashion houses of Avenue Montaigne, this Aveyron bistro has been feeding the neighborhood since 1923. It is the kind of place to order what the southwest does best: escargots or bone marrow to start, then lamb shoulder or duck confit. Book by phone, and come on Friday, because Chez Savy opens Monday to Friday only and is closed at weekends. Dinner is served from 19:00 to 23:00.

stops.name: Le Bar du Plaza Athénée
stops.text: Finish around the corner at the Plaza Athénée, where the bar sits under a deep blue fabric ceiling around a counter cut from a single block of resin. Have a glass of Champagne, or a long drink built on cognac or calvados, and watch the room fill up after dinner; there is often a DJ. The dress code is elegant, so leave the sneakers at the hotel. On Fridays it stays open until 2:00, and it will be busy with people coming back from the rugby.

days.title: Saturday: the Latin Quarter in winter sun
days.intro: The oldest garden in Paris turns 400 this year. Start there, then work west through the Middle Ages and end in a jazz cellar on the rue de la Huchette.

stops.name: Jardin des Plantes and the Grande Galerie de l'Évolution
stops.text: The Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle is celebrating 400 years in 2026, and Saturday's forecast of sun and light wind is perfect for its garden. Walk the long avenues of plane trees first, then go into the Grande Galerie de l'Évolution, where a procession of stuffed African animals crosses the floor under an iron and glass roof. Until March 7 the gallery also shows *Artistes au Muséum*, paintings made for and about the collections. Adult tickets are €16; book a time slot online. The Grande Galerie closes on Tuesdays, not Saturdays.

stops.name: La Mosquée de Paris restaurant and tearoom
stops.text: Across the road from the garden, the Grand Mosque's restaurant serves couscous, tagines, pastilla and grilled kefta. After lunch, move to the tearoom for mint tea with baklawa and cornes de gazelle at about €2 each, according to Paris Zigzag. On a sunny day, sit out on the mosaic patio; otherwise stay inside. The tearoom runs all day, so it also works as a mid-afternoon stop. You can book a table on the restaurant's website.

stops.name: Musée de Cluny: Nicolas Flamel
stops.text: Walk west along the rue des Écoles to the national museum of the Middle Ages, in a Gothic abbots' mansion built against Roman baths. Its autumn show, *Nicolas Flamel, alchimiste de papier*, runs until January 24 and separates the real Parisian scribe from the alchemist of legend (and of Harry Potter). Keep time for the six *Lady and the Unicorn* tapestries in their own dim room. Tickets are €14 and free for visitors under 26; open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:30 to 18:15.

stops.name: Shakespeare and Company
stops.text: The English-language bookshop facing Notre-Dame is crowded on Saturdays, but the late afternoon is when the light goes and the lamps come on among the shelves. Climb to the reading room upstairs, then buy something stamped with the shop's seal. Next door, the café does an espresso for €3 and a hot chocolate for €6, a good warm-up after the walk along the river. If the queue to get in is long, it moves; the café is the place to wait for someone browsing.

stops.name: Allard
stops.text: Cross the boulevard Saint-Michel for dinner at Allard, an old-school bistro now run by Alain Ducasse's group. This is a night for the dishes made to share: duckling with olives (€110 for two) or roast Bourbonnais chicken (€92 for two), with a half-dozen escargots first. It is open every day for lunch and dinner. Book by phone; Saturday night fills early.

stops.name: Caveau de la Huchette
stops.text: Five minutes away, down a staircase into a vaulted cellar, is the swing and jazz club where Parisians have danced since the 1940s. On Saturday the singer Eboni Fondren is on from 21:30, and the floor is soon full of dancers who clearly practise; nobody minds if you just watch from the benches with a beer. Seats are sold at the door, without reservations, for about €10 to €16. The nearest metro, Saint-Michel on line 4, is closed; use Cluny–La Sorbonne or the RER.

days.title: Sunday: the 12th arrondissement, from the market to the movies
days.intro: A neighborhood Sunday east of the Bastille: the city's best-loved market, a walk on an old railway viaduct, a long lunch and an afternoon with Belmondo.

stops.name: Marché d'Aligre and Marché Beauvau
stops.text: Sunday morning is when the 12th does its shopping. The street stalls of rue d'Aligre sell fruit and vegetables cheaply and loudly, and in the middle of the square stands the covered Marché Beauvau, with cheese, fish and charcuterie under its timber roof. The small flea market on the square is the place for old postcards and kitchenware. Go early, as the open-air market runs from 7:30 to 14:30 on Sunday, and bring cash and a bag.

stops.name: Coulée verte René-Dumont
stops.text: A few streets south, an old railway line runs on top of the brick arches of the Viaduc des Arts, and its track bed is now a planted path above the traffic. Climb up near avenue Daumesnil and walk east, looking down into the apartments and courtyards on either side, until the path drops into the Jardin de Reuilly. It is the gentlest way to see this part of the city. Sunday is the day forecasters were least sure about, with a small chance of a few drops of rain, so keep this walk in the morning.

stops.name: Le Square Trousseau
stops.text: Back by the market, this corner brasserie on the little Square Trousseau is open every day of the week, Sunday included, from 8:30 in the morning. It is the neighborhood's Sunday lunch: steak tartare, a sea bass tartare, or poularde with morels if you want to settle in. Ask for a table by the window. Reservations are recommended at weekends; call ahead.

stops.name: Belmondo, le magnifique at the Cinémathèque
stops.text: Take line 14 two stops to Bercy for the afternoon indoors, in Frank Gehry's tilted building at the edge of the Parc de Bercy. The Cinémathèque's big show on Jean-Paul Belmondo runs until January 31: clips, posters and photographs from *Breathless* onwards, phones that play his famous lines and a green screen where you can try his stunts. Tickets are €14. On Sunday it is open 11:00 to 20:00; afterwards, check the day's screenings, since its cinemas show films from the archive all weekend.

stops.name: Amarante
stops.text: End the weekend near the Bastille at Christophe Philippe's small bistro, a serious kitchen that, unusually, opens on Sunday night (it closes Wednesdays and Thursdays instead). The cooking is old-school and unapologetic: grilled veal brain or crisp Kintoa pig's trotters to start, then pigeon with its giblets and boudin, and a dark São Tomé chocolate fondant to finish. Michelin lists it among the city's best Sunday tables. The room is small, so book.

stay.name: Hôtel de Crillon
stay.text: The 18th-century palace on Place de la Concorde, commissioned under Louis XV and run by Rosewood, was ranked No. 14 on The World's 50 Best Hotels list in October. It has 124 rooms and suites, including the Grands Appartements designed by Karl Lagerfeld, and a spa. This weekend it is perfectly placed: Friday's plan is a walk up the Champs-Élysées gardens, and the Tuileries Christmas market opens on Saturday just across the square.

stay.name: L'Hôtel
stay.text: The small hotel on rue des Beaux-Arts where Oscar Wilde died, with rooms around a tall circular stairwell and a mosaic swimming pool under stone vaults in the cellar. Le Wilde's bar hosts jazz evenings. It is a short walk to Saturday's dinner at Allard and the Latin Quarter, and an easy ride to the Grand Palais.

stay.name: Hôtel Paradiso
stay.text: The cinema chain mk2's hotel on boulevard Diderot gives every room a projector, a big screen and proper sound, with a library of about 10,000 films, plus a rooftop bar. It is a fun base for a weekend that ends at the Cinémathèque, and it is in the 12th, so Sunday's market, viaduct walk and dinner are all close by.

events.name: Paris Photo
events.text: The world's biggest fair for photography fills the nave, balconies and salons of the Grand Palais, in the bicentenary year of the medium. Tickets are sold online until the fair opens.

events.name: France v South Africa
events.text: France's fifth match of the 2026 Nations Championship, against the world champions. Tickets from €35. RER D is suspended northbound that evening; take RER B to La Plaine–Stade de France or line 14 to Saint-Denis Pleyel.

events.name: AOP Festival
events.text: Free festival of 52 protected-origin dairy products, 47 of them cheeses, with a producers' market, tastings, cooking demonstrations and evening DJ sets. Workshops are booked on site.

events.name: Rencontres du ciel et de l'espace
events.where: Cité des sciences et de l'industrie, 19th
events.text: An astronomy fair with sky-watching workshops, planetarium sessions, talks and a sale of telescopes and equipment.

events.name: Tuileries Christmas market opens
events.text: About 95 chalets and rides between Concorde and the rue de Rivoli, with a big wheel of almost 80 meters, an ice rink, mulled wine and regional food. Free entry; until January 3.

events.name: Faubourg Saint-Honoré Christmas lights
events.text: The luxury shopping street switches on its Christmas lights. The theme had not been announced by November 9.

events.name: Boulogne-Billancourt Half Marathon
events.where: Boulogne-Billancourt and the Bois de Boulogne
events.text: About 13,000 runners on a flat course along the Seine and through the Bois de Boulogne; expect road closures just west of Paris.

know: **From CDG:** RER B runs to Gare du Nord and Châtelet–Les Halles in roughly 35 to 50 minutes, on the special airport ticket, and no weekend closures are listed on the airport branch. Official taxis charge a fixed fare to the Right Bank and a slightly higher one to the Left Bank, posted at the rank; allow 45 minutes to an hour, longer on Friday evening.
**From Orly:** Metro line 14 runs from the airport to Châtelet, Pyramides and Saint-Lazare, with no closures announced this weekend. It also serves Bercy, the stop for Sunday's Cinémathèque visit.

**Tickets and closures:** A single metro ticket is €2.55 on a Navigo Easy card from any station machine. Saint-Michel on line 4 is closed until December 19 and République on line 8 until April 22, 2027. **Line 13 is closed along its whole length on Sunday morning until noon,** line 12 is cut north of Jules Joffrin on Saturday and Sunday, and RER D runs no trains between Gare du Nord and Gare de Lyon all weekend. Station closures are usually announced the day before; check the RATP app.

**Rugby night:** France play South Africa at the Stade de France at 21:10 on Friday. RER D is suspended northbound that evening, so RER B and line 14 will be crowded towards Saint-Denis before the match and back into Paris afterwards.

**Protests:** The Yellow Vests' national coordination has called an "Act V" for Saturday, November 14, backing other marches that day rather than organizing its own procession. No Paris route or time had been published by November 8. Check the RATP app on Saturday morning before heading to the Latin Quarter.

**November 13:** Friday is the anniversary of the 2015 attacks. Small ceremonies and flowers are usual at the memorial garden on Place Saint-Gervais behind the Hôtel de Ville, at the Bataclan, and outside the cafés on rue de Charonne, rue Bichat and rue Alibert. Be considerate around these places.
**Tipping:** Service is included in French bills by law. Rounding up for a coffee, or leaving a few euros after a good dinner, is a courtesy, not an obligation.

**Weather and light:** Monday's forecasts were dry and sunny but cold on Friday and Saturday, from about 2°C at dawn to 9°C in the afternoon, then milder and cloudier on Sunday with a slight chance of rain. It is dark soon after 17:00.
